posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: Make an 'L' shape with two mirrors. If you suspect green sensitivity, cut a small piece of the film in a dark environment and place it on the base of the L. Then place a small coin over the film and zap the film with a green laser so the laser covers both arms of the L. If it is green sensitive, then you should get a grating everywhere except where the coin was. If it was not green sensitive, you won't get a grating at all. A small piece of film and a relatively heavy coin should provide enough stability for a weak grating.

> **PinkysBrain:** What's the advantage of the PVA/water/monomer approach vs say Sergio's approach? It needs a wet development step right?

Sergio's does not need wet processing. In fact, as far as I'm aware, no polymer needs wet processing, which is it's great advantage. PVA is simply a carrier, much like gelatin, into which you put your photosensitive material which actually cross links actinically (is that how you spell it?) with the PVA, that is, PVA is not actinic in and of itself. I suppose you could make the argument that photosensitive polymers are also not actinic in and of themselves, so that there us no conceptual difference between a photosensitive polymer and PVA (or gelatin, for that matter). You could also argue that the polymer itself may undergo actinic reactions. Martin and Sergio are probably the best people to determine that difference.

However, from all reports (never actually tried the stuff), PVA has low sensitivity; Jeff Blyth claims 7 mJ/cm^2 ( [http://river-valley.tv/pva-photopolymer ... olography/](http://river-valley.tv/pva-photopolymer-for-classroom-holography/) ). I believe the emulsion has to be pretty thick, but I get this from reports by Nadia working with Yuri Denisyuk and they may have made it thick for a specific application. 

I believe Danny has tried PVA. He might be able to comment some more

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** "10% PVA" mentioned in the recipe above means 90% water and 10% PVA polymer right?

Yes, although whether by weight or volume, I don't know. I assume by volume. If the densities were equal, it wouldn't make any difference, but I don't know the density of PVA.

> **PinkysBrain:** the PVA (and the water) is merely a scaffold, the migration/polymerization of the acrylamide within it records the hologram I think.

Yes, I believe you're right, which is why I mentioned the difference between a "carrier" of sorts that acted as a "host" for actinic reactions, as opposed to actually being actinic in and of itself. Photoresist, for example, is actinic in and of itself, while gelatin is not.

> **PinkysBrain:** As far as the wet development, I think the PVA solution needs wet development ... that's why I asked what the advantage is. UV development ala Sergio's solution seems so much easier.

I may have misunderstood the question. If you're asking why dry development has an advantage over wet development, it's primarily because of swelling. Wet development changes the physical structure of the emulsion, whereas dry development just changes the phase relationships in the emulsion, not the physical structure. So, in wet development, swelling causes a shift in reconstruction angles for transmission holograms and a colour shift in reflection. Also, it creates bandwidth. Dry development causes no shift in wavelength and has very low bandwidths. In effect, dry development is better in one way for colour work, where swelling is an important factor. However, the lack of bandwidth may be a problem for colour because the human visual system reacts to bandwidth almost as much as it reacts to wavelength. Your eye cannot see very low bandwidths and interprets colour by bandwidth as much as central frequency. 

Another effect may be brightness, since, as I said above, bandwidth is an important factor in the total luminosity of a hologram. So, the efficiency of a dry-developed hologram may be high, but still be visually dim because the bandwidth is too low. In this case, the material is very good for HOEs. Of course, another advantage of high efficiency/low bandwidth is in a master-copy setup. In such a system, high efficiency/low bandwidth is very advantageous, so long as the copy medium has a high bandwidth.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **PinkysBrain:** What's the advantage of the PVA/water/monomer approach vs say Sergio's approach? It needs a wet development step right?

Quite right, our materials don't require wet processing (see [http://www.polygrama.com](http://www.polygrama.com)). 

One issue with the above formula may be that it might be limited to low spatial frequencies only. So I assume it will be difficult to record reflection holograms. At the same time I'm aware there are PVA/acrylamide mixtures that allow the recording of reflection holograms. But usually they require a special PVA plus an additonal crosslinker.

As for liquid processed photopolymers, principally many kinds of monomer mixtures may be used. Index modulation can become very high and large bandwidths à la DCG can be obtained (see also the materials introduced by Polaroid or Canon).

The only – albeit serious – drawback is the liquid processing step...

On the other hand, regarding dry systems, it used to be a huge challenge to provide them with high index modulation and relatively large bandwidth at moderate speed. Most research seems to focus on ever more complicated monomer mixtures/initiators (to squeeze out yet another few fractions of a percent of enhanced index change).

We tried a completely different approach. We're about to launch a new material that may at least partially meet those above mentioned requirments. Our new experimental stuff called DAROL essentially relies on a 19th century technology (sorry I can't be more specific!). Taking interest in nearly forgotten photographic processes turned out to be useful – even to nowadays' photopolymer world.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **dannybee:** Taking interest in nearly forgotten photographic processes turned out to be useful – even to nowadays' photopolymer world.

Not just the photopolymer world. My paper at HoloPack in Toronto in '08 dealt with the idea of using dcg as a resist material. I managed to get a dcg hologram with the characteristics of a resist hologram with better efficiency than a resist that could be electro-formed. This came from the idea of the Carbon Black printing process - another 19th century technology!

I also remember in the early 80's the standard bleaches (for 8E and 10E75) were Ferric Nitrate, Van Ranesse/dichromate and Ferricyanide. I wondered whether permanganate would work as a bleach. Not knowing enough about processing chemistry, I never got it to work well. Then I met an older guy who told me that permanganate bleaches were well known to photographers from the the early 20th century. This time, I was trying to reproduce a forgotten technology that I didn't know even existed!

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **dannybee:** being that the permanganate is purple Or vilot i would think that would put it into the iR range

No. At, least, not in terms of observed colour.The colour of an object is what's "thrown out" after it's absorbed some of the spectrum. Permanganate is purple, so I assumed that "not purple" would be red. I forgot that purple is a mix of red and blue, so it may have been absorbing green and "throwing out" red and blue. That's not to say that it doesn't absorb in the IR, but it's not valid to say that it must absorb in IR because it's coloured purple.

 I had talked about permanganate as a possible for a red sensitive "dcg", since I thought it was absorbing red. I even thought of haemoglobin as a red sensitive additive, but that's another story; I haven't bled for holography yet! I was in India while Joy was still here. She had to coat some plates for a client and asked me if it was OK to try and coat a few plates with permanganate. She asked how much and I said try the usual amount of dichromate. Anyway, she told me that there was a purplish crust over the whole plate but she said she'd shoot them anyway. A few days later, while I was still in India, she emailed that there was nothing in red, but there was something - not much of something, but something - at 532. I asked her what made her try 532 and she said that when 633 didn't work out, she tried 457, 514 and 532! I would not have bothered. I'd have just said, "Oh well, it doesn't work at 633" and let it go at that. When I got back from India and saw the purple crust, I realised I'd have to go down to about 1/10th of the amount of permanganate she'd used. This time I got about 20% odd efficiency with 532.

posts.content_md:
Danny's link showing the plot of permanganate is interesting in that it shows a very prominent green absorption. Permanganate should be red, according to the plot. It brought to mind that Maxwell made the first tri-chromatic photograph (*Maxwell: Proc Roy Inst, 3, p370*) using three colour filters. However, Vogel discovered the use of sensitising dyes 25 years later. So, it was always a problem as to how Maxwell recorded red. It turns out that a lot of red dyes emit in the UV *(Evans, C. H. and Smith R. B. J. : Soc. Mot. Pic. Tel. Eng. 65, p365, 1956)*. So it's believed that Maxwell's red filter actually transmitted UV, which the emulsion was responsive to. I'm wondering if the purple appearance of permanganate is also due to this reason.
